newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bejart celebrates 70th birthday with Lausanne bash.
newsitem.headline: Bejart celebrates 70th birthday with Lausanne bash.

text.p: French choreographer Maurice Bejart launched celebrations for his 70th birthday at the weekend, surrounded by his star dancers, family and celebrity friends.

Bejart, who turns 70 on January 1, was the first on stage at a gala on Friday evening before a glittering crowd of 1,000. He performed excerpts from his own spoof ballet "The Imaginary Moliere," first given at the Comedie Francaise 20 years ago in Paris.
"Thank you for coming, I love you," Bejart, dressed in his signature black t-shirt and trousers, told the audience.

Italian baritone Ruggero Raimondi, Farah Pahlavi, the wife of the late Shah of Iran, actress Annie Chaplin, Hugues Gall, director of the Paris Opera, and Bejart's sister Claude Cauchois Vergez and her children were among his guests.

A dozen modern dances were performed during the multi-media event, including a piece from Bejart's latest work "The Clergy House has lost none of its Charm, and the Garden none of its Lustre" set to the song "Let me Live" by the rock group Queen.
The 25 lithe dancers wore costumes, mainly in white with some black splashes, by Italian designer Gianni Versace.

Bejart's latest work, which had its world premiere last week in the Swiss city, is a tribute to Queen singer Freddie Mercury and Argentinian dancer Jorge Donn, a Bejart protege best remembered for his solo of Bolero, music by Maurice Ravel.
"Jorge Donn had great affection for Freddie Mercury. Both went wild on the stage in the same way. Both died of AIDS at age 45, exactly a year apart," Bejart told reporters recently.
French dancer Patrick Dupond, formerly director of dance at the Paris Opera who now performs as a guest soloist, stole the show with his world creation of "La Tuile" (What a Blow).
Dressed in blue gym clothes, Dupond improvised female roles and mocked classical repertory, including Swan Lake, then massaged his sore calves and asked: "How do the girls do this?"
Long-legged French dancer Sylvie Guillem performed a spell-binding duet with Marc Spradling, a piece called "Herman Schmerman", by American choreographer William Forsythe.
Carolyn Carlson, a blond American dancer, performed her own piece, "The Fenice which burned down", recalling the fire which ravaged the 18th-century Venice theatre last January.

Carlson then closed the show with two other dancers in a tribute to Bejart entitled "For you", with lyrics by Dwight Carlson: "If not for you, I'd be nowhere at all. I'd be sad and blue, if not for you."

Red rose petals fell on the stage at the finale, and white streamers spelling "Happy Birthday Maurice" hung from the ceiling of the Metropole theatre as Bejart bowed with the cast. A midnight dinner and Saturday brunch rounded off the weekend.
Among dancers in the audience were Tania Bari, who danced in 1959 in the Marseille-born Bejart's first major creation, "The Rite of Spring", set to music by composer Igor Stravinsky.
The dancers went on the next year to form his 20th Century Ballet in Brussels, which thrived for more than 25 years.

In 1987 Bejart brought the troupe to Lausanne, which offered better conditions and subsidies. He opened with "Souvenir of Leningrad", with music by Tchaikovsky. Recent creations include "1789 and Us", "Death in Vienna" and "Mr C" (Charlie Chaplin).

French actress Marie Trintignant read a work by Apollinaire and the audience viewed an excerpt from the 1964 film "The Green Queen" starring Spanish-born French actress Maria Casares, a close friend who died last month, and Frenchman Jean Babilee.
